Reviewer #1:

This study tracks the evolution of 205 S. cerevisiae populations over roughly 10,000 generations. In brief, the authors confirm observations emerging from previous, similar experiments in yeast and E. coli, with populations showing a declining increase in fitness over time and various complex interactions between sub-populations in the same population, as well as between mutations in the same genome.

While some of the findings reported in this particularly eloquent manuscript are perhaps not completely novel, the study distinguishes itself from previous work by its vast scale (number of populations and generations, as well as comparing haploids vs. diploids) and the comprehensive analyses, which together yield a more integrative view on the different evolutionary forces and mechanisms at play. As such, I believe that the report furthers our understanding of evolution, and perhaps in particular domestication.

One major difference with the LTE experiment in E. coli is the size of the populations. Would this explain some of the observed differences? I believe this could use a bit more discussion.

The different adaptive dynamics and patterns in haploids and diploids is perhaps the most interesting and most novel part of the study, and I believe that this merits more attention in the Discussion section. The authors carefully consider different possible reasons for the slower adaptation observed in diploids, as well as the potential role of LOH and sex (including inbreeding). The idea that inbreeding could help purge deleterious heterozygous hitchhiker mutations is particularly interesting and might even explain why yeast cells have evolved the mating type switching system that promotes inbreeding (apart from the fact that it also makes it easier for cells to escape the haploid form after a sporulation event, which can be crucial to survive famine and other stressful environments). I wonder whether the authors can comment a bit more on these aspects. Moreover, the quick and likely irreversible loss of the capacity to go through a sexual cycle may also tell us that lab evolution experiments are very far removed from evolution in nature, since most wild strains show efficient meiosis. Domesticated industrial yeasts, on the other hand, show very similar patterns of evolution, suggestion that domestication of industrial microbes is in fact very similar to the directed evolution experiments carried out in labs (e.g. my lab's own work: DOI:https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.020 )

Discussion: The rise of mutator phenotypes might also depend on the levels and nature of selective pressure imposed on the cells? Conditions that severely hamper growth (and thus the supply of mutations), or stress conditions that require the combined effect of two (or more) mutations may be more prone to drive the evolutionary success of mutators? See for example DOI: 10.7554/eLife.22939.

Reviewer #2:

I read with interest the manuscript "Phenotypic and molecular evolution across 10,000 generations in laboratory budding yeast populations". It adds to our understanding of experimental evolution by providing one of the longer running experiments, here using a eukaryote (Saccharomyces cerevisiae). As the authors note, previous experiments of a similar length (>=10,000 generations) have been conducted with bacteria (especially the LTEE experiment of Lenski and colleagues).

The manuscript is generally well written, and I believe deserving of a major publication with broad readership. A few larger suggestions are to discuss more thoroughly the following points:

1) One of the biggest puzzles in my mind is why the authors didn't see more polyploidization. As noted by Harari et al., 2018, and found in many previous long-running experiments (starting with Gerstein et al., 2006, and many others noted in Table 1 of Fisher et al., 2018), spontaneous diploidization is common in experimental evolution studies with yeast. Given that there was such a large initial fitness advantage to diploids (Figure 2), the fact that only one line diploidized over a much longer time span is interesting. Is this something peculiar to the strain or the environmental conditions (I didn't see anything that would have selectively maintained haploids in the Materials and methods, although the lines were constructed to be able to selectively maintain haploids versus diploids). Harari et al. studied several strains, so it isn't obvious that the W303-derived strain used here would differ.

2) A main result is the diminishing nature of the fitness gains. This is certainly not surprising, and I believe the result, but I was surprised that this was not quantitatively tackled. One of the biggest questions addressed from the LTEE is whether fitness approaches an asymptote or continues to increase at a slowing rate. It is almost certainly too early to address this question definitively, but fitting different functions and noting what can or cannot be rejected at this stage would be a welcome addition to the paper.

3) Similarly, it is claimed that the variability among lines decreases (subsection “Fitness changes during evolution”), but this is neither statistically confirmed nor visually obvious in Figure 2.

4) When discussing the lack of mutators, perhaps also note the difference in ancestral mutation rates. S. cerevisiae has a larger genome-wide mutation rate than E. coli (Lynch et al., 2016), which would have decreased the advantage to rare mutators.

5) Another major difference from the LTEE is said to be the lack of coexisting strains. I'm not convinced that this is a qualitative difference. Coexistence is only possible once the period of strongly adaptive sweeps is over (i.e., where the fitness benefit of any adaptive mutation falls below the fitness difference between the coexisting strains). Given the strong signs of adaptive mutations seen in Figure 3 (including the supplement), it could well be that there are plenty of mutations that could coexist, but that hitchhiking has eliminated them. Only once fitness gains have really slowed might they be seen to persist.

6) It is claimed in the Discussion at the authors find only "one strong case of repeatability at the level of the nucleotide change", but this hasn't actually been discussed in the text. Which case are they referring to? There are several listed Figure 5—figure supplement 1. Also, the reader cannot tell whether contamination is a possible source of the repeated hits in this supplementary figure. Please discuss.

Other comments:

1) The first page of the Introduction is too generic and could be cut or shortened.

2) The claim made in the text that "We find a different pattern in some diploid populations, where an initial slower period of fitness gain is succeeded by a significant rapid increase in fitness" is not supported by the data presented. I would move Figure 2—figure supplement 1B to Figure 2 as an second row of panels. Even then, as presented in these additional panels, the diploids only appear to adapt rapidly later on in SC30; this might be because of the course division into halves of the experiment in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B (would thirds be clearer?), but at any rate the statistical evidence for this claim needs to be added.

3) Related to the above point, one of the main explanations for why diploid adaptation is expected to speed up is if the available beneficial mutations are partially recessive, giving a small boost when in heterozygotes but only a large boost in fitness once an LOH event occurs. This is of interest, but it requires showing statistically that there is an acceleration in fitness gain in the diploids, which is not clear.

4) Introduction and subsection “Patterns of molecular evolution specific to diploids” – A direct comparison of haploid and diploid rates of adaptation was conducted by Gerstein et al., 2011, [The Marad experiment is good to cite, but the haploid and diploid experiments weren't contemporaneous and only in one environment. The Fisher et al. experiment isn't really as relevant to this point but is very relevant to the routes of adaptation accessible to haploids versus diploids and the difference in autodiploidization rates.]

5) "agreement with this hypothesis" – The finding of slow then fast adaptation is not in agreement with the hypothesis in the previous sentence that diploids adapted more slowly because they started at a higher fitness. That hypothesis does not explain why diploids would speed up.

6) Subsection “Molecular evolution” and elsewhere – In all comparisons with results from previous results (especially LTEE), please provide the generation at which a comparison can be made (ideally at 10,000). Results from LTEE that didn't appear until much later aren't reliably a difference from the current experiment. This is touched upon in the Discussion but is needed at first mention.

Lynch, M., Ackerman, M. S., Gout, J. F., Long, H., Sung, W., Thomas, W. K., and Foster, P. L. (2016). Genetic drift, selection and the evolution of the mutation rate. Nature Reviews Genetics, 17(11), 704.

Reviewer #3:

1) Please make explicit how generations are calculated. Is this estimated number of generations per week on each media updated with the empirical results of fitness assays? Or simply assumed to remain constant?

2) Please clarify the rationale for varying the reference strain for calculating fitness among environments in the text. (Presumably, a concern about sensitivity for fitness assays at different absolute fitness.)

3) In competitive fitness assays, it is more ideal to have both strains marked with a fluorescent marker for the reason the authors highlight-fluorescent genotypes will typically produce a small non-fluorescent subset in the population-but given the design here, running the assay with one marked strain is fine. I miss some detail in the supplement about the nature of the fitness calculations, and it does not appear the authors have provided the raw ratios of the flow cytometry data used to calculate fitness. The availability of the code for analysis of this data is noted in the Transparent Reporting document, but it would be helpful to make the information more prominent in the manuscript text.

4) Relatedly, in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, there appear to be a set of strains in the SC 37°C environment that showed low fitness in replicate 2 compared to replicate 1. This is not necessarily problematic given the scale of the analysis presented here, but as written the manuscript is somewhat opaque about exactly what technical (or biological) variation could contribute to this pattern. Please clarify by providing the raw fitness measurements and/or by addressing this small discrepancy directly.

5) It might be helpful to readers to annotate the pathway in Figure 7A with the frequency of mutations in each gene.

6) The majority of the beneficial ade2 stop codon reversions observed are in diploids. The authors make the case for target size of the stop codon reversion (vs. hitting of other parts of the pathway) making a difference to the frequency with which populations find the functional ADE fitness peak. Is a difference in target size for haploids and diploids relevant here?

7) It would be helpful provide a brief description of the mutual information inference for readers.

claims.claim: Within the first 10,000 generations of the LTEE, 4 of the 12 populations fix mutator alleles, and 3 of the 12 populations have coexisting lineages detectable from sequencing data.
claims.source: However, we note that within the first 10,000 generations of the LTEE, 4 of the 12 populations fix mutator alleles, and 3 of the 12 populations have coexisting lineages detectable from sequencing data.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a comparison to the LTEE.

claims.claim: The lack of mutator lineages may stem from a difference in the rate at which mutators arise or a different balance between the relative importance of beneficial and deleterious mutations.
claims.source: Instead, the lack of mutator lineages may stem from a difference in the rate at which mutators arise or a different balance between the relative importance of beneficial and deleterious mutations (which depends on the environment and ancestral fitness; see e.g. Swings et al., 2017 and Kryazhimskiy et al., 2014) that leads to less indirect selection for mutators (Good and Desai, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis with citations.

claims.claim: The yeast strains have mutation rates that are higher than the ancestral E. coli strain in the LTEE, though lower than the LTEE mutator lineages.
claims.source: We also may have less second-order selection for mutators in our experiment because our strains have mutation rates that are higher than the ancestral E. coli strain in the LTEE, though lower than the LTEE mutator lineages (Lang and Murray, 2008; Wielgoss et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations.

claims.claim: The yeast strains and environments may lack the metabolic pathway architecture to produce cross-feeding or other interactions that could be the basis for coexistence.
claims.source: Our strains and environments may simply lack the metabolic pathway architecture to produce cross-feeding or other interactions that could be the basis for coexistence.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis.

claims.claim: Coexisting lineages may have emerged but been lost due to drift or strong within-lineage adaptation.
claims.source: Alternately, coexisting lineages may have emerged in our experiment but been lost due to drift or strong within-lineage adaptation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an alternative hypothesis.

claims.claim: The yeast populations are smaller than those in the LTEE, so low-frequency lineages will be lost more commonly during the daily bottleneck.
claims.source: Since our populations are smaller than those in the LTEE, low-frequency lineages will be lost more commonly during the daily bottleneck.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a comparison to the LTEE.

claims.claim: The evolution of mutation rates and of stable ecological interactions may not be as general or widespread as the LTEE has suggested.
claims.source: Regardless of the reasons for these differences, our results suggest that the evolution of mutation rates and of stable ecological interactions may not be as general or widespread as the LTEE has suggested, and may instead vary substantially based on differences in the organisms or details of the environmental conditions.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the findings.

claims.claim: Haldane's sieve slows adaptation in diploids.
claims.source: The dynamics of mutations in the adenine biosynthesis pathway provides a particularly interesting example of both how Haldane's sieve slows adaptation in diploids and how diploids can bypass the sieve by loss of heterozygosity.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the ADE pathway dynamics.

claims.claim: Diploids can bypass Haldane's sieve by loss of heterozygosity.
claims.source: The dynamics of mutations in the adenine biosynthesis pathway provides a particularly interesting example of both how Haldane's sieve slows adaptation in diploids and how diploids can bypass the sieve by loss of heterozygosity.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the ADE pathway dynamics.

claims.claim: Most diploid populations homozygously fix a loss-of-function mutation upstream in the ADE pathway at some point during the experiment.
claims.source: At some point during the experiment, most of our diploid populations homozygously fix a loss-of-function mutation upstream in the pathway, which eliminates the deleterious toxic intermediate produced as a result of the ancestral ade2-1 mutation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claims.claim: Haploids typically fixed ADE pathway mutations earlier in the experiment than diploids.
claims.source: While the rate of loss of heterozygosity was high enough to produce these genotypes and expose them to selection, it appears to have been a limiting factor; haploids typically fixed these mutations earlier in the experiment (Figure 3—figure supplements 1–9).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding with figure references.

claims.claim: 4/6 populations with the ade2-1 reversion mutation are diploids.
claims.source: Haldane's 'speedcheck' here slowed adaptation but also provided diploid populations with more time to search for the single-codon target of the (highly beneficial and apparently dominant) ade2-1 reversion, and indeed, 4/6 populations with this mutation in our experiment are diploids.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claims.claim: Long-term adaptation to a constant environment can be characterized by widespread clonal interference, contingency, and steady molecular evolution even as fitness increases slow down over time.
claims.source: Our results here reinforce the conclusion that long-term adaptation to a constant environment can be characterized by widespread clonal interference, contingency, and steady molecular evolution even as fitness increases slow down over time.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claims.claim: The results highlight the role of dominance and loss of heterozygosity in diploid evolution.
claims.source: They also highlight the role of dominance and loss of heterozygosity in diploid evolution.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claims.claim: The work calls into question the generality of conclusions about the importance of the evolution of mutation rates or stable coexistence.
claims.source: However, our work also calls into question the generality of conclusions about the importance of the evolution of mutation rates or stable coexistence.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

results.result: The authors established a long-term evolution experiment with 205 S. cerevisiae populations (124 haploid and 81 diploid) evolved for ~10,000 generations across three environments (YPD 30°C, SC 30°C, SC 37°C) using batch culture with daily dilutions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C11-C14 provide comprehensive experimental design details including population numbers, ploidy types, environments, culture conditions, and population losses. The methodology is clearly described with specific dilution ratios and generation counts, providing a well-documented experimental framework.

results.result: Most populations exhibited declining adaptability with rapid fitness increases in early generations followed by slower adaptation, though some diploid populations in SC 30°C showed an initial slow period followed by rapid fitness increases.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C15, C16, C73, C74 describe fitness trajectory patterns supported by Figure 2 data. The general pattern of declining adaptability is well-documented across most populations, with the exception of specific diploid populations showing alternative dynamics. Statistical support and visual evidence strengthen these observations.

results.result: Haploid populations gained more fitness than diploid populations on average (p<0.02), with diploids having higher ancestral fitness in all environments. MATa haploids evolved more rapidly than MATα haploids in SC 30°C (p<0.02).
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C20 present statistically significant findings with p-values and cite consistent prior work. The observations are supported by Figure 2 data and Mann-Whitney U tests. The interpretation considers both Haldane's sieve and declining adaptability as potential explanations.

results.result: Mutations accumulated steadily through time across all sequenced populations, with populations fixing mutations linearly even late in the experiment.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C21, C76 describe the temporal pattern of mutation accumulation supported by Figure 3 sequencing data. The steady, linear accumulation of fixed mutations is clearly demonstrated across 90 focal populations over six timepoints, providing strong evidence for continuous molecular evolution.

results.result: Widespread genetic parallelism was observed at the gene and pathway level, with populations predictably adapting through mutations in the adenine biosynthesis pathway, sterility-associated genes, and negative regulators of the Ras pathway, though only one case of nucleotide-level parallelism (ade2-1 reversions) was found.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C35-C36, C77-C79 demonstrate parallelism supported by Figure 5-6 data showing excess high-multiplicity genes and GO term enrichment. The distinction between gene/pathway-level parallelism (widespread) and nucleotide-level parallelism (rare) is well-documented. Statistical analyses and null model comparisons strengthen these conclusions.

results.result: Historical contingency was observed through over-dispersion of mutations ('coupon collecting') and elevated mutual information between multi-hit genes (p=0.036), indicating that mutations in certain genes affect the likelihood of mutations in others.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C52-C55 present statistical evidence for contingency through over-dispersion analysis and mutual information calculations (Figure 7 supplements). The p=0.036 for total mutual information provides modest but significant support, though individual gene pairs lack sufficient power for detection.

results.result: No long-term coexistence of lineages or populations with highly elevated mutation rates were observed, contrasting with findings from the E. coli LTEE.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C23-C24, C80-C81 report negative findings supported by Figure 3 data showing continuous fixation without stable coexistence. The contrast with LTEE is appropriately contextualized with claim C82 noting that even in LTEE, these phenomena took time to emerge. The absence of evidence is well-documented through sequencing data.

results.result: Populations with dramatically elevated mutation rates were not observed, with only one potential mutator event (P1E11) showing a modest increase in indel mutations likely due to an MSH3 mutation.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C32-C34 document the absence of strong mutator phenotypes with Figure 3B and Figure 4 supplement 2 showing no sudden increases in mutation accumulation rates. The single exception (P1E11) is characterized as modest, contrasting with the dramatic increases seen in LTEE. The evidence is thorough and appropriately qualified.

results.result: MATa populations showed consistently higher mutation accumulation rates than MATα or diploid populations, likely due to a TSA1 G146S mutation in the MATa ancestor that increases mutation rate approximately 5-fold.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C29 present a clear causal chain from observation (higher mutation rate in MATa) to hypothesis (TSA1 mutation) to experimental validation (Figure 4 supplement 1 fluctuation assays). The lower dN/dS ratio in MATa populations (significant in SC 37°C, p<0.01) supports increased hitchhiking. The reconstruction and validation in BY4741 background strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Fixed mutations showed dN/dS ratios near one, with approximately 45-50% missense, 40-45% synonymous/noncoding, and 5-10% nonsense/indel mutations across strains and environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 describe the distribution and selection signatures of fixed mutations supported by Figure 4A-B. The dN/dS near one is interpreted as balance between beneficial selection and hitchhiking/purifying selection. The consistency across environments and strains strengthens these observations.

results.result: Evolution in diploid populations involved both fixation of heterozygous mutations and frequent loss-of-heterozygosity (LOH) events, with LOH patterns affected by both recombination hotspots (e.g., rDNA array on chromosome XII) and selection for recessive beneficial mutations (e.g., ADE pathway mutations). Haldane's sieve slowed diploid adaptation but could be bypassed through LOH.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C59-C60, C89-C92 describe diploid-specific evolutionary dynamics supported by Figure 8A showing genome-wide LOH patterns and Figure 3 showing ADE pathway dynamics. The dual role of recombination rates and selection in shaping LOH patterns is well-documented. The ADE pathway provides a clear example of how LOH bypasses Haldane's sieve, though haploids still fixed these mutations earlier.

results.result: Diploid populations accumulated substantial recessive deleterious load, with heterozygously fixed mutations including a large percentage of high-impact mutations in essential genes and higher proportions of high-impact mutations in non-essential genes compared to haploid or homozygous diploid fixations.
results.evaluation: Claims C58, C61-C62 present evidence for deleterious load supported by Figure 8B-C showing enrichment of high-impact mutations in essential genes among heterozygous fixations. The comparison across haploid, diploid LOH, and diploid non-LOH categories is systematic. However, C58 notes that genetic reconstructions or backcrossing would be needed for full characterization, appropriately qualifying the conclusions.

results.result: The W303 ancestral strain carries an ade2-1 mutation causing toxic AIR accumulation. Almost all populations fixed loss-of-function mutations upstream of ADE2 to prevent toxicity, while five populations fixed rare reversion mutations restoring ADE2 function, achieving higher fitness. The rarity of reversions (6/205 populations) reflects the small mutational target size of single-codon reversion versus multiple genes for upstream loss-of-function.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C51 describe the ADE pathway dynamics supported by Figure 3A, Figure 6, Figure 7, and prior work (C45-C46 cite Kokina et al. 2014, Sharma et al. 2003, Rojas Echenique et al. 2019). The fitness landscape interpretation (Figure 7B) and target size explanation for reversion rarity are well-reasoned. The observation that reversion populations don't fix upstream LOF mutations (C50) provides internal consistency.

results.result: A few populations experienced dramatic fitness increases due to ade2-1 reversion mutations, with 4 of 6 such populations being diploids, suggesting that Haldane's sieve provided diploids more time to find this rare beneficial mutation.
results.evaluation: Claims C17 and C93 connect the high-fitness populations (marked with asterisks in Figure 2) to ADE2 reversions and note the diploid enrichment. The interpretation that slower diploid adaptation provided more time to search mutational space is creative and plausible, though somewhat speculative. The observation is well-documented but the mechanistic explanation could benefit from additional support.

results.result: Most multi-hit genes showed mutations distributed across strains and environments, but several genes showed strain- or environment-specific enrichment (e.g., SRS2 and LCB3 in SC 37°C, CCW12 in diploids).
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C41 describe patterns of parallelism specificity supported by Figure 6 and statistical tests described in methods. The identification of environment- and strain-specific effects uses appropriate likelihood ratio tests with multiple hypothesis correction. Examples are clearly documented in the data.

results.result: Some genes with 10 or more hits had no high-impact mutations fixed, with several being essential genes, suggesting selection for change- or gain-of-function rather than loss-of-function.
results.evaluation: Claim C43 identifies an important exception to the general pattern of loss-of-function mutations in multi-hit genes, supported by Figure 6 data. The inference about change- or gain-of-function is reasonable but would benefit from functional validation. The observation is well-documented but the mechanistic interpretation remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: Only one focal haploid population underwent whole genome duplication during the experiment, contrasting with previous studies showing frequent diploidization in evolving haploid yeast populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 report a surprising negative finding supported by Figure 8 supplements 1-2 showing ploidy analysis. The contrast with prior work (Gerstein et al. 2006, Fisher et al. 2018, Harari et al. 2018) is appropriately noted. The low frequency could reflect experimental conditions (unshaken cultures, specific environments) but the observation is well-documented.

results.result: CCW12 is a candidate for overdominance, with preferential hits in diploids and only 2 of 17 fixed mutations losing heterozygosity, though prior work (Leu et al. 2020) found mixed evidence for overdominance.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 present CCW12 as a candidate for overdominance based on diploid enrichment and low LOH rate (Figure 6). However, C63 is explicitly speculative and C64 notes that Leu et al. 2020 did not detect overdominance in reconstructions. The evidence is suggestive but insufficient to confirm overdominance without genetic reconstructions, as acknowledged in C58.

results.result: The mitochondria was maintained in all populations, but frequent loss or loss-of-function occurred in the 2-micron plasmid and killer virus components. By generation ~10,000, 89/90 populations lost killing ability, with loss occurring most rapidly at high temperature, likely due to segregation/replication failure and toxin inactivation at elevated temperatures.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C70 describe extrachromosomal element dynamics supported by Figure 9A showing killer phenotype loss and citations to prior work. The temperature effect is consistent with previous studies (Jerison et al. 2020, Woods and Bevan 1968, Weinstein et al. 1993). The mechanistic explanations are well-supported by literature, though the authors did not sequence viral genomes to confirm the mechanism in their populations.

results.result: The 2-micron plasmid was lost less frequently in diploid strains and most consistently and rapidly in the high-temperature environment.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 describe 2-micron plasmid dynamics supported by Figure 9B. The patterns parallel killer virus loss, suggesting similar temperature sensitivity. The diploid effect is interesting but not mechanistically explained. The observations are well-documented through copy number analysis.

results.result: Clonal interference was frequently observed, with groups of mutations rising to high frequency and then declining due to competition with other lineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C22 and C75 describe clonal interference patterns supported by Figure 3A allele frequency trajectories showing multiple competing lineages. The observation is consistent with theoretical expectations for asexual populations of this size and is well-documented across multiple populations.

results.result: Mutations in negative regulators of the Ras pathway are commonly observed in yeast evolution experiments and have been shown to be beneficial in similar environments.
results.evaluation: Claim C37 contextualizes findings with prior literature (Rojas Echenique et al. 2019, Kryazhimskiy et al. 2014, Lang et al. 2013, Venkataram et al. 2016). This is appropriate citation of established knowledge in the field and helps interpret the parallelism observed in the current study.

results.result: The lack of mutator lineages and stable coexistence in this experiment, compared to the LTEE, may reflect differences in mutation rate, balance of beneficial/deleterious mutations, metabolic pathway architecture, population size effects on drift, or other organism/environment-specific factors, suggesting these phenomena may not be as general as the LTEE suggested.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C88 present multiple hypotheses for differences from LTEE, appropriately noting the speculative nature (C83, C85, C86 are marked as speculation/inference). While the hypotheses are reasonable and cite relevant theory (Swings et al. 2017, Kryazhimskiy et al. 2014, Good and Desai 2016), they remain untested. The conclusion about generality (C88) is appropriately qualified but goes beyond what the negative findings alone can support.

results.result: Long-term adaptation to constant environments can be characterized by widespread clonal interference, contingency, and steady molecular evolution despite slowing fitness increases, with dominance and LOH playing important roles in diploid evolution. However, the generality of conclusions about evolution of mutation rates and stable coexistence is questioned.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C96 synthesize the major conclusions of the study. C94 and C95 are well-supported by the collective evidence from fitness trajectories, sequencing data, and diploid-specific analyses. C96 appropriately questions generality based on the contrast with LTEE, though this conclusion is somewhat limited by the negative nature of the findings and lack of mechanistic resolution.

results.result: The LTEE has been conducted for over 30 years and 70,000 generations with 12 E. coli populations in the same constant environment.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10 accurately describe the LTEE with appropriate citation (Lenski 2017). This provides essential context for comparing the current yeast experiment to the most prominent long-term evolution experiment.
